en: She is the very soul of a man.
This great woman Aychürök
Is the khan of womankind.
Gather the settled peoples
Of Jeti-Özön, filled with Jediger;
There is no sieve over the people’s mouths—
Restrain your gossiping nation.
Let no rude-tongued troublemaker
Call her a captive woman.
Let Aychürök not hear, become enraged,
And fly in fury to the city
Of her father Akun Khan;
Let her not gather an army from Afghanistan,
An immense force no easy thing to face,
With pale hazy banners like mountains,
With piercing cries and rallying shouts,
With a roaring battle tumult,
Mounted and armed upon gray stallions,
Carrying mottled gray war standards,
And wage war without restraint.
Let them not fight summer and winter,
Stand packed together in battle,
Choice horses dying among the herds,
The people shaken and heroes killed,
The nation subjected to suffering,
All its champions ruined.
Let there be no further conflict;
Take care, friend Kyyaz,
Let there be no such quarrel.
Do not reproach her by accident;
Hero, do not treat her as your equal in anger.
Approve whatever she says
And keep inclining your neck to her.
Leave her in peace for six years,
Then slowly make her your wife.
Submit to what she says,
Give her whatever she desires,
And cherish the dear woman Chürök
Above all your people.
Cast a cold lasso
On countless horses no petitioner could obtain;
Take the beautiful woman Chürök yourself,
And do not leave her dejected.
Win Chürök through hardship,
And take her as your gift.
Champion, raise the hero Kanchoro
As khan over the world!”
All the Jediger together
Now seated the hero Kanchoro
Upon a white felt rug.
With a plane-tree garden around him,
A golden throne in the tower,
They placed a golden crown upon him,
Raised him onto the golden throne,
And proclaimed him khan.
To the walled fortress,
To Chachykey’s palace,
News came that brave Semetey had died,
Had seen the true place
From which none returns,
That the dear man had passed away.
Yesterday, when he scattered great wealth,
When brave Semetey, the mighty gray wolf,
Set out toward Talas,
He had gathered eight khojas.
The aged khan, ruler of Bukhara,
Had given her to him while she was a maiden;
She was his maternal aunt.
This spoiled woman Chachykey
Was Semetey’s wife.
She summoned the messenger
Who had brought the news and said:
“If what you say is true,
If it is sound and not a lie,
I will consent to what you ask;
I will give you sixty camels
As your reward for glad tidings.”
Calling quickly upon Baabedin,
The woman glowed with delight:
“My khan Kanchoro will take me!”
All her sorrow disappeared,
All her grief was mended;
The woman brightened and recovered,
All her resentment dissolved,
Her burning heart grew calm.
“Yesterday, while the bloodthirsty lord still lived,
I knew much anguish;
Kanchoro and I
Would whisper together.
We had pledged
To camp freely on the ridge
And become husband and wife.”
The spoiled woman Chachykey—
So much was the shameless one esteemed;
The scoundrel had attained
Her promise and desire.
“Take gold for your glad tidings,
Gold scattered in fist-sized pieces.”
She rejoiced when her lord died—
Such was Chachykey’s nature.
Her wickedness stood revealed;
The woman rejoiced
That she would marry Kanchoro.
That woman Chachykey,
That swaggering infidel,
Slaughtered ninety colts for her feast
And set her wealth against the cost.
She let the Jediger overrun
Semetey’s great stronghold;
She had bright gold and white silver
Scattered in lavish handfuls,
And gathered khojas and mullahs.
That woman Chachykey
Had Kanchoro cut up the meat;
She made the splendid entertainment
Surpass that of all the people.
As for saintly old Bakay,
She had eighty fearsome wrestlers
Drag him about as their kökbörü carcass,
Neither killing nor losing him.
Though not eighty but a thousand
Used brave Bakay for kökbörü,
Your khanly uncle would not yield.
From ancient times until now,
That uncle had endured torment.
All his coat was torn,
All his beard was plucked,
All his armor was stripped,
And every whisker of your aged uncle Bakay
Was torn from his face.
As the wrestlers mauled him,
Behold your ancestor like Bakay,
Your prophet-like uncle,
Parted from those who loved him;
Behold how he was humiliated.
His swan-white beard turned pale;
Your ancestor stood withered.
Bereft of those who loved him,
Behold what that grave-robbing wretch
Did to your father.
Tears from both eyes spread in ten streams;
Unable to die though wishing for death,
Your ancestor went about weeping.
Deprived of those who would sustain him,
Your poor uncle Bakay—
Behold how he wailed.
His face wrinkled and wasted;
Tears flowing from both eyes
Poured across his breast.
The broad world became narrow;
Majestic Bakay became old and gray.
What is seen today is gone tomorrow—
Such filth this world proves to be!
His insides burned, his heart was gone;
He had no strength to exchange blows.
He stooped, and strength left his back;
From your uncle Bakay’s hands
All courage fled, all power departed.
Certain that he would die,
The wretched old man mounted in this state.
Sweet words had left his mouth;
The wide, staring eyes
Had left your ruined uncle.
All vigor fled from Bakay;
This was when he sank deep into misery.
He had no life beyond lying still;
This was when Bakay lay upon his side,
His only loved one gone,
While Kanchoro dragged him as a kökbörü carcass.
Brave Bakay went rolling
Along the path of the stallions;
Brave Bakay passed through the hands
Of seventy Jediger wrestlers.
The broad world became narrow;
Great Bakay could no longer join counsel.
Parted from his children,
He was subjected to peculiar disgrace.
That costly cap of blue lynx—
Who had not worn it jauntily?
When people saw the lion Bakay,
All beneath moon and sky would tremble.
Now an iron cage surrounded him,
And thick misery lay upon Bakay Khan.
Bakay the lion, victor in many races,
Became their kökbörü carcass that day.
“While my fortune was intact,
I was a man of lofty purpose.
Akbaltay, forefather of this servant,
How long were you there?
Alas, may my only one survive,
May that soul never witness such humiliation!
In the prime of strength and longing,
While my only one remained alive,
Tall, broad-shouldered,
Both wrestler and lion,
He was a glowing red ember,
Peerless in my world;
My Morning Star companion of the moon,
My honored sultan,
The light for my grieving soul,
My keepsake left
By Albambet who passed to the other world.
He girded his belt with skill;
If seven divisions of black foes appeared,
He entered alone and attacked.
The choicest of the falcons,
My Külchoro was precious.
May my sole loved one not die;
As my final journey draws near,
May my orphaned loved one not die,
And may Bakay not see this grief!
Ah, have I, Bakay,
Eaten the flesh of the mythical zymyryk bird?
Parted from my champions,
Did you decree long ago
That I should burn to death?
In old age, have I, Bakay,
Fallen into a clamor unlike all others?
Did I drink the water of immortality?
Wretched soul who has strayed so often,
Did you eat the raven’s eye?
At every time and in every age,
My beloved Creator,
Did you decree that Bakay should wither and die?
My gentle gray-mottled falcon,
My Morning Star, my gray hawk,
My one plane tree before me,
The misty tower above my head,
My one leopard, do not die;
May this frail soul never see such grief!
While fortune was upon my head,
I, saintly old Bakay,
Was known as a hero.
I, Bakay, it seems,
Have eaten my fill to the very snout.
Rather than lay this grief upon my head,
God, why did you not take me before I grew old?
Rather than lay this torment upon my head,
Why not leave me lying swollen in this earth?
Kanchoro, who has blinded my eyes—
Why did I not gouge out yours?
Why did I not slaughter you
And leave you no life
When you were still an infant?
The saintly princess Kanykey
Had spoken prophetic words:
If he survived, she said,
He would prove an enemy at heart.
When he sucked the breast, blood flowed;
His appearance was strange,
For at heart he was an enemy.
A clamor rose from his heart;
The words spoken by the wretched princess
Have proven true.
I, Bakay, failed to take care,
And swung this way and that;
